pr_title: journal: Reset runtime seqnum data when flushing to system journal
pr_body:
The current system journal's seqnum ID will usually be different from the seqnum ID of the current runtime journal. Therefore, to avoid unnecessary rotations on boot, reset the runtime seqnum data when switching to system journal so that systemd-journald will adopt the system journal's seqnum ID and value on next write.

Fixes: https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/30092

> i am not sure i follow. the idea so far was that it is benefical having a single series of seqnums for the whole boot, hence we carry that over. why get away from that?

Unfortunately that's inherently incompatible with not rotating the journal every boot (which is important for storage space efficiency) since we don't know the system journal's seqnum ID until flush to `/var`, unless we somehow store the current seqnum data somewhere accessible when journald is started in initramfs (maybe efivars?)

Also AFAIK during flush to `/var` the entries copied from runtime journal to system journal should continue the seqnum of the rest of system journal so this isn't really a problem unless you want to transfer journal entries to an external host during early boot and be able to order those entries against ones made later in boot by seqnum.

@poettering 
> i am not sure i follow. the idea so far was that it is benefical having a single series of seqnums for the whole boot, hence we carry that over. why get away from that?

With this patch,
1, On early boot stage, journald generate new seqnum ID, and starts new seqnum series.
2. On flush to /var/, the persistent seqnum ID is picked to the mmap. And runtime journal entries are copied to persistent storage with the persistent seqnum ID and new seqnum.

So, the issue #30092 is fixed.

> (and at the very least, this is not material to sneak into rc4)

I previously moved the original issue to v256 even though it is a regression, as I thought that it is hard to fix. But it _can_ be fixed in such a simple way. And already tested. I do not think we should postpone this PR.

@msizanoen1 
> unless you want to transfer journal entries to an external host during early boot and be able to order those entries against ones made later in boot by seqnum

At least, systemd-journal-remote does not use seqnum and seqnum ID. So, should not be a big problem, unless a custom importer is used.

> Hold on - does this mean there are no longer sequential numbers through the boot process? Because that's an issue if so

This does not lose seqnum stability.
On early boot, journal entries are stored in runtime journal, and seqnum is started from 1.
On flushing journal after '/' is (re)mounted rw, the runtime journal entries will be saved with new seqnum after the last seqnum in the persistent journal, and thus it is not necessary to rotate journal on flush.
As you can see, such scenario is now well tested by the test case added in this PR.

issue_context.title: Journal file rotation because of different sequence number ID
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

254.5

### Used distribution

Gentoo

### Linux kernel version used

6.5.11-gentoo

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

systemd-journald

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

The user journal file from the previous boot should be used.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

User log rotation happens. The kernel log reports this:

    systemd-journald[856]: /var/log/journal/xxxxxxx/user-xxxxx.journal: Journal file uses a different sequence number ID, rotating.

This happens on 3 different machines with the same systemd version.

### Steps to reproduce the problem

Version 254.4 seems to have this issue.

### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

```sh
The contents of journald.conf:

[Journal]
Storage=auto
Compress=yes
SystemMaxUse=2G
```
